title: AISG's primary consideration
learningObjective: Explain the principle that guides AISG decisions about suspected abuse or neglect.
scenario: A team is deciding how to respond to a concern, and several competing interests are being discussed.
question: Which consideration must guide AISG's decision first?

answerOptions.text: Protecting the school's reputation while facts are gathered
The interests and welfare of the child
Avoiding disruption to the student's timetable
Reaching agreement with every adult involved

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG states that the interests and welfare of children are the primary consideration in decisions about suspected abuse or neglect.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Other factors may need attention, but AISG's commitment statement puts the child's interests and welfare first.

title: Four main areas of abuse
learningObjective: Identify the four main areas of student abuse named by AISG.
question: Which four areas are identified in the handbook as the main areas of student abuse? Select all that apply.

answerOptions.text: Neglect
Physical abuse
Sexual abuse
Psychological or emotional abuse
Academic underperformance
Ordinary friendship conflict

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG identifies neglect, physical abuse, sexual abuse, and psychological or emotional abuse as the four main areas.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Academic performance or ordinary conflict may prompt support, but they are not listed as the four main areas of abuse.

title: Recognising affluent neglect
learningObjective: Recognise that neglect can occur in affluent households.
scenario: A student arrives well dressed and often receives expensive gifts. They regularly describe being left without emotional support and under extreme pressure to succeed because caregivers are rarely available.
question: What is the most appropriate interpretation?

answerOptions.text: Material comfort rules out neglect
This may indicate affluent neglect and should not be dismissed
It is only a concern if the student's grades decline
The student should first confront their caregivers

correctFeedback: Correct. The handbook notes that absent caregivers, gifts replacing love and care, and extreme pressure can be signs of affluent neglect.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Neglect can be present despite material wealth and may be under-recognised when outward needs appear to be met.

title: Indicators require professional attention
learningObjective: Interpret possible indicators without assuming or dismissing abuse.
scenario: Over several weeks, a student becomes unusually withdrawn, flinches when an adult approaches, and gives inconsistent explanations for bruising.
question: What is the safest professional judgement?

answerOptions.text: These signs prove physical abuse, so question the student until the cause is known
The signs may have other explanations, but together they create a concern that should be reported
Wait until a caregiver confirms what happened
Ignore the bruising unless the student directly asks for help

correctFeedback: Correct. Indicators may have other causes, but employees report reasonable concerns rather than investigating or waiting for proof.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Signs do not prove abuse, but they must not be dismissed. Report the concern through AISG's safeguarding pathway.

title: Every professional has a role
learningObjective: State who is responsible for protecting student welfare at AISG.
scenario: A staff member notices a concerning change but assumes safeguarding is only the counsellor's responsibility.
question: What does the handbook require?

answerOptions.text: Only counsellors and school leaders need to act
Every professional who comes into contact with students has a safeguarding role
The staff member should wait for a colleague with specialist training
Only the student's classroom teacher can raise a concern

correctFeedback: Correct. Protecting students' welfare is the role of every professional who comes into contact with students at AISG.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Specialist teams lead the response, but every employee is responsible for recognising and reporting concerns.

title: Student-on-student abuse
learningObjective: Recognise the scope of student-on-student abuse.
question: Which statements match AISG's definition of student-on-student abuse? Select all that apply.

answerOptions.text: It can include physical, sexual, emotional or financial abuse and coercive control
It can occur between classmates, friends or romantic partners
It can happen at school, at school events or outside school
It only counts when an adult is directly involved
It must be repeated before it becomes a safeguarding concern

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG's definition covers several forms of harm, varied student relationships, and incidents in or outside school.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Student-on-student harm is not limited to repeated incidents or incidents involving adults.

title: Antagonistic behaviour
learningObjective: Recognise behaviour included in AISG's antagonistic behaviour definition.
scenario: A group repeatedly excludes a student from shared activities and sends threats that the student must pay them to be left alone.
question: How should this be understood?

answerOptions.text: As ordinary friendship conflict to be resolved informally
As possible antagonistic behaviour involving exclusion, threats and extortion
As a concern only if physical injury occurs
As a private matter outside staff responsibility

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG includes threats, extortion or blackmail, and purposeful exclusion in antagonistic behaviour.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Harmful exclusion, threats and extortion fit AISG's examples of antagonistic behaviour even without injury.

title: Cyber harassment beyond school
learningObjective: Recognise cyber harassment as a safeguarding concern.
scenario: Students use a private messaging group after school to spread abusive rumours and threatening messages about another student.
question: What is the most appropriate response?

answerOptions.text: Treat it as outside AISG's concern because it happened after school
Recognise possible cyber harassment and report the concern
Ask the targeted student to leave the group and take no further action
Post a warning in the same group from a personal account

correctFeedback: Correct. Cyber harassment includes abusive or threatening messages, rumours, and group-based abuse using technology.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. AISG recognises student-on-student harm outside school and cyber harassment through messaging systems and social media.

title: AI-generated harmful media
learningObjective: Identify AI-generated or manipulated harmful media as cyber harassment.
scenario: Students create a convincing AI-generated image that falsely depicts a classmate in a humiliating situation and begin sharing it.
question: Which judgement best matches the handbook?

answerOptions.text: It is harmless if everyone knows the image is fake
It may be cyber harassment because manipulated media can misrepresent or harm someone
It is only an IT issue unless posted publicly
Staff should ask students to delete it but should not record the concern

correctFeedback: Correct. The handbook specifically includes creating or sharing AI-generated or manipulated media that misrepresents or harms another person.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. The fact that media is synthetic does not remove the harm; AISG explicitly includes harmful deepfakes within cyber harassment.

title: A report about another student
learningObjective: Respond appropriately when a student reports harm by another student.
scenario: A student says another student has been sending sexually explicit requests and pressuring them to respond.
question: What should you do next?

answerOptions.text: Arrange a meeting between both students to establish the truth
Listen calmly, avoid investigating, record the student's words and report to the appropriate SSL
Tell the student to block the sender and return only if it happens again
Contact the other student's caregiver before telling anyone at school

correctFeedback: Correct. Student-on-student sexual harm is a safeguarding concern. Respond supportively, record accurately and report through AISG's pathway.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Do not mediate, investigate or contact caregivers independently. Preserve the student's account and report it promptly.
handbookSection: 3.2 Student on Student Abuse; 4.1 Reporting Requirements

title: First response to a disclosure
learningObjective: Demonstrate the correct immediate response to a student disclosure.
scenario: A student stays behind after class and quietly says, 'Something happens at home that scares me.'
question: What is the best immediate response?

answerOptions.text: Show alarm so the student understands the seriousness
Remain calm, listen carefully and let the student speak in their own words
Ask a series of detailed questions before the student changes their mind
Tell the student to return with a written statement

correctFeedback: Correct. Remain calm, listen without prompting, and allow the student to tell their story without your assumptions.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Shock, pressure or detailed questioning can make disclosure harder and can influence the student's account.

title: Avoid leading questions
learningObjective: Distinguish listening and clarification from leading or investigative questioning.
scenario: A student says, 'They hurt me yesterday,' but has not said who 'they' are.
question: Which response is most appropriate?

answerOptions.text: 'Was it your caregiver who hurt you?'
'Tell me what you mean by they.'
'They have done this before, haven't they?'
'I need you to prove that before I can help.'

correctFeedback: Correct. A neutral request for clarification avoids supplying an answer or imposing an assumption.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Leading questions suggest details. Use only neutral clarification needed to understand the student's words; do not investigate.

title: Supportive language
learningObjective: Use supportive, non-investigative language during a disclosure.
scenario: A student has begun describing possible neglect and appears worried that speaking up was wrong.
question: Which responses align with the handbook? Select all that apply.

answerOptions.text: Tell the student they are doing the right thing by speaking to an adult
Let the student know they are believed
Promise that nothing difficult will happen next
Explain that you will do your best to protect and support them
Ask the student to repeat the account to several colleagues

correctFeedback: Correct. Reassure the student that speaking was right, that they are believed, and that you will seek protection and support.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Be reassuring without making promises you cannot guarantee or causing the student to repeat details unnecessarily.

title: No promise of secrecy
learningObjective: Explain confidentiality honestly when a student asks for secrecy.
scenario: Before disclosing, a student says, 'Promise you won't tell anyone.'
question: What is the safest response?

answerOptions.text: Promise secrecy so the student feels safe enough to continue
Explain that you may need to tell specific people who can help, while keeping the matter as confidential as possible
Stop the conversation until the student agrees in writing
Say that every member of staff will need to be told

correctFeedback: Correct. Do not promise secrecy. Explain that certain people must be told to help, and that information will be kept as confidential as possible.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. A promise of secrecy cannot be kept when safeguarding action is needed; equally, the matter must not become general knowledge.

title: Record and report accurately
learningObjective: Sequence the actions that follow a student disclosure.
scenario: A student has finished sharing a concern. They are comfortable and not in immediate danger.
question: Place the next actions in the safest order.

answerOptions.text: Record what the student said in their own language, including dates and times
Report to the appropriate Division Student Safeguarding Lead
Maintain confidentiality and follow the safeguarding process

correctFeedback: Correct. Record the student's words and relevant details, report promptly to the appropriate SSL, and keep the matter confidential throughout follow-up.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Preserve an accurate account first, report it promptly through the AISG pathway, and maintain confidentiality.
handbookSection: 4.1 Responding to a Disclosure; 4.2 Reporting Pathways

title: Reasonable cause is enough to report
learningObjective: Apply AISG's mandatory reporting threshold.
scenario: You have reasonable cause to believe a student may be at risk of abuse, but you do not have proof.
question: What must you do?

answerOptions.text: Wait for proof so the report cannot be challenged
Report the suspected incident in accordance with AISG procedures
Investigate privately before deciding
Ask colleagues to vote on whether it seems serious

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG requires employees to report whenever they have reasonable cause to believe a student has suffered or is at risk of abuse or neglect.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Proof is not the reporting threshold. Waiting or investigating can delay protection and is not the employee's role.

title: Immediate danger
learningObjective: Escalate immediately when a student may be in immediate danger.
scenario: A student describes a situation that leads you to believe they are at risk of suffering significant harm today.
question: What should you do next?

answerOptions.text: Finish the day and submit a report when convenient
Contact the appropriate Student Safeguarding Lead immediately and communicate the concern through the safeguarding process
Call the caregiver first to check the student's account
Contact external agencies independently before informing AISG

correctFeedback: Correct. The reporting pathway requires immediate contact with the appropriate SSL when you believe a student is at risk of significant harm.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Do not delay, contact caregivers independently, or bypass AISG's safeguarding lead. Escalate to the SSL immediately.

title: A non-urgent concern
learningObjective: Use the reporting pathway for a concern that is not an immediate emergency.
scenario: You notice a pattern that gives reasonable cause for concern, but the student appears safe at this moment.
question: Which action best follows AISG's reporting pathway?

answerOptions.text: Record the observations and report the concern through the safeguarding system and appropriate SSL
Wait until the pattern becomes an emergency
Ask the student to collect evidence
Discuss the pattern with several colleagues before reporting

correctFeedback: Correct. Record observations, follow AISG's reporting procedures, and consult the appropriate SSL; urgency changes speed, not the duty to report.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. A non-emergency concern should still be recorded and reported. Do not wait for escalation or broaden disclosure.

title: A colleague asks you not to report
learningObjective: Maintain personal reporting responsibility when another adult asks for silence.
scenario: A colleague tells you something that creates reasonable cause for concern, then says they will handle it and asks you not to report.
question: What should you do?

answerOptions.text: Assume the colleague will report and take no action
Report the concern yourself through AISG's safeguarding pathway
Keep the information private to preserve trust with the colleague
Wait a week and ask whether the colleague followed up

correctFeedback: Correct. Every employee has a reporting responsibility; you should not assume another person will fulfil it.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. A colleague's request does not remove your duty. Report when you have reasonable cause for concern.

title: Need-to-know confidentiality
learningObjective: Protect confidentiality after reporting a concern.
scenario: After reporting, people who are not part of the safeguarding response ask what happened.
question: Which actions follow the handbook? Select all that apply.

answerOptions.text: Do not discuss the incident with other staff who are not involved
Do not share details with family or loved ones
Allow the safeguarding team to manage information on a need-to-know basis
Give close colleagues a summary without using the student's name
Post a general warning in a staff chat

correctFeedback: Correct. Confidentiality means limiting details to those managing the safeguarding response, not discussing the incident more widely.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Removing a name does not make broad discussion appropriate. Do not share with uninvolved staff, students, people outside school or loved ones.

title: A private student conversation
learningObjective: Maintain transparency when individual time with a student is necessary.
scenario: A student asks to discuss a sensitive issue privately after class.
question: Which arrangement best follows the Employee Code of Conduct?

answerOptions.text: Use a locked room so the conversation cannot be overheard
Meet out of earshot but within sight of others, and let another adult know where you are
Drive the student somewhere quiet in your own car
Use a room with covered windows to protect privacy

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG expects private conversations to remain observable, with others aware of where the adult and student are.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Privacy does not require secrecy. Maintain sight lines, avoid enclosed hidden spaces, and tell another adult where you are.
handbookSection: 6.4 Appropriate Relationships; 6.5 Professional Roles around Children

title: Safe Touch decision
learningObjective: Apply AISG's Safe Touch expectations.
scenario: During PE, brief physical guidance could help a student learn a safe movement.
question: Which conditions should guide the decision? Select all that apply.

answerOptions.text: The touch has a clear educational purpose
It is in the student's interests and conducted publicly
Gender considerations and whether the touch is wanted are taken into account
The adult may touch areas normally covered by a swimsuit if the lesson is important
The touch may be kept secret to avoid embarrassing the student

correctFeedback: Correct. Safe Touch must serve a clear purpose, be in the student's interests, respect consent and gender considerations, and occur publicly except in emergencies.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Touch must never be secret or involve swimsuit-covered areas for ordinary instruction. It must be necessary, respectful and visible.

title: Entering a student bathroom
learningObjective: Apply AISG's bathroom and changeroom access protocol.
scenario: You hear signs that a student may be at risk inside a student-designated bathroom. It is concerning but not an extreme emergency.
question: Place the actions in the safest order.

answerOptions.text: Get a partner and attempt gender-matched entry
Announce who you are and why you need to enter
Enter to address the concern
Report the entry to the Student Safeguarding Lead as soon as possible

correctFeedback: Correct. Except in an extreme emergency, enter with a partner, announce yourself and the reason, address the concern, then report the entry to the SSL.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Students' safety permits entry, but the protocol requires transparency, a partner where possible, and prompt self-reporting afterward.

title: A low-level adult conduct concern
learningObjective: Report an adult conduct concern without deciding the harm threshold personally.
scenario: You notice an adult repeatedly arranging unnecessary one-to-one time with one student. You cannot say it meets the harm threshold, but it creates a nagging doubt.
question: What should you do?

answerOptions.text: Wait until you can prove misconduct
Share the concern with the principal under the Adult Conduct Concerns protocol
Challenge the adult publicly and investigate their history
Discuss it informally with several colleagues first

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG expects even small adult conduct concerns or nagging doubts to be shared; the Principal and School Safeguarding Coordinator determine the threshold.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. You do not need to classify or prove the behaviour. Share the concern through the protocol so patterns can be identified and assessed.
handbookSection: 7.1 What is an Adult Conduct Concern?; 7.3 Reporting Protocol

title: Proactive self-reporting
learningObjective: Self-report a situation that could be misinterpreted or fell below expected conduct.
scenario: A sudden event left you alone with a student in circumstances that could look compromising, even though no harm occurred.
question: What should you do next?

answerOptions.text: Say nothing because your intentions were appropriate
Proactively self-report in person to the SSL or divisional principal
Ask the student to confirm in writing that nothing happened
Only report if another adult witnessed the situation

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG expects proactive self-reporting of situations that may be misinterpreted or fall below the Code of Conduct standard.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Self-reporting protects transparency and allows the situation to be recorded appropriately; it does not imply wrongdoing.

title: Choosing a communication channel
learningObjective: Choose a school-authorised channel for school-related communication.
scenario: A student sends you a school-related question through your personal social media account.
question: What is the most appropriate response?

answerOptions.text: Continue the conversation because the topic is school-related
Move the communication to an authorised school account such as Outlook or Microsoft Teams
Reply from a personal email account instead
Ask the student to create a private group chat

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG requires official school accounts for school-related communication and prohibits one-to-one social media or personal email contact with students.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. School-related content does not make a personal channel appropriate. Move the conversation to an authorised school channel.

title: Caregiver contact on WeChat
learningObjective: Apply AISG's social media expectations to caregiver communication.
scenario: A caregiver messages your personal WeChat account about an individual student's progress and invites you to join the grade-level caregiver group.
question: What should you do?

answerOptions.text: Reply in WeChat because caregiver contact is less restricted than student contact
Redirect the conversation to an authorised school channel and do not join the grade-level group unless you are a caregiver of that grade
Join the group but avoid posting
Ask another caregiver to relay school information

correctFeedback: Correct. School matters belong on authorised channels. Employees should not join grade or class caregiver WeChat groups unless they are a caregiver of that grade.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Personal social media is not an authorised channel for individual school matters with caregivers, and grade-level groups have specific restrictions.
handbookSection: 8.3 Social Media - Communication; School Official Context

title: Student privacy in photography
learningObjective: Protect student identity and images in personal and educational photography.
scenario: You have photos from a school activity and a short video used to give a student feedback.
question: Which actions align with AISG expectations? Select all that apply.

answerOptions.text: Do not post recognisable student faces on a personal social media account
Use authorised school channels and applicable consent rules for educational photography
Delete feedback photos or videos immediately after the feedback session
Post student initials with the photo because initials are not identifying
Assume caregiver permission to the school also covers an employee's personal account

correctFeedback: Correct. Personal accounts must not show student faces or identifiers; educational media belongs on authorised channels, and feedback media is deleted after use.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Caregiver permission to AISG does not extend to personal accounts, and the handbook treats student names and initials as identifying information.
handbookSection: 8.3 Social Media - Privacy and Personal Information; 6.9 Aquatics Photography

title: Overnight curfew check
learningObjective: Apply safeguarding expectations during overnight-trip room checks.
scenario: During an overnight trip, two chaperones conduct a curfew check. One student is in the shower when they arrive.
question: What should the chaperones do?

answerOptions.text: Accept a roommate's confirmation that the student is present
Return in five minutes and re-check so every student is seen face to face
Enter the bathroom to confirm immediately
Skip that room and record the student as present

correctFeedback: Correct. If a student is showering or using the restroom, chaperones return in five minutes and re-check; all students must be seen face to face.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. Privacy must be respected while ensuring accountability. Return and complete a face-to-face check.
handbookSection: 9.1 Student Safeguarding Procedures for Overnight Stays

title: When something does not feel right
learningObjective: Act on a nagging doubt about adult conduct.
scenario: Nothing you observed clearly proves harm, but an adult's pattern of interaction with a student leaves you with a persistent sense of unease.
question: What is the most appropriate final judgement?

answerOptions.text: Keep watching until the behaviour meets the harm threshold
Share the adult conduct concern through AISG's protocol, even if it seems small
Ask the student directly whether the adult is abusive
Ignore intuition because only documented incidents can be reported

correctFeedback: Correct. AISG defines an adult conduct concern broadly enough to include a small concern, sense of unease or nagging doubt.
incorrectFeedback: Not quite. You do not need to investigate or decide the threshold. Sharing a concern is a neutral safeguarding act that allows appropriate review.
handbookSection: 7.1 What is an Adult Conduct Concern?
